New directions in the study of prime ideals in rational, nilpotent Iwasawa algebras

Adam Jones    William Woods
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Let GG be a nilpotent pp-valuable (compact pp-adic Lie) group. There is an ongoing investigation into the prime ideals of its completed group algebra (Iwasawa algebra) ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[[G]], and there remains an open conjecture that they can all be proved to have a canonical standard form. We very this conjecture for several new classes of nilpotent groups, including those corresponding to the positive subalgebra of almost all classical and exceptional types, curiously excluding those of type CC. †† 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 22E35, 22E27, 20C07, 16W70, 16W80, 17B22

1 Introduction

Fix a prime pp. and let GG be a pp-valuable group in the sense of [10] (see Definition 2.5 below). This is a torsion-free, pro-pp group, isomorphic (as a topological group) to a closed subgroup of some GLn​(ℤp)\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}_{p}) consisting of upper-triangular matrices congruent to the identity mod pp (if p>2p>2) or mod 44 (if p=2p=2).

Let RR be a commutative pseudocompact ring. The completed group algebra (also known to number theorists as the Iwasawa algebra) of GG over RR is defined as

R⁡[[G]]=lim←U⁡R⁡[G/U],R[[G]]=\varprojlim_{U}R[G/U],

where R⁡[G/U]R[G/U] is the ordinary group algebra of the (finite, discrete) group G/UG/U with coefficients in RR, as UU runs over the set of open normal subgroups of GG.

Now fix a finite extension of fields K/ℚpK/\mathbb{Q}_{p}, with ring of integers 𝒪\mathcal{O}, uniformiser π\pi, and residue field k=𝒪/πk=\mathcal{O}/\pi. There is an ongoing investigation into the prime ideals of 𝒪​G:=𝒪⁡[[G]]\mathcal{O}G:=\mathcal{O}[[G]], especially when 𝒪=ℤp\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}, beginning with the paper [1], and advanced in several subsequent articles, including [3], [4], [7], [9],[2] and [12].

We say that a prime ideal PP of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G is standard if we can find a closed normal subgroup HH of GG such that G∗:=G/HG^{*}:=G/H is pp-valuable and the image of PP under the surjection 𝒪​G→𝒪​G∗\mathcal{O}G\to\mathcal{O}G^{*} is centrally generated. We say that PP is virtually standard if P∩𝒪​UP\cap\mathcal{O}U is standard for some open subgroup UU of GG [9, Definition 1.1].

The main conjecture in the study of prime ideals in Iwasawa algebras (see e.g. [9, Conjecture 1.2]) roughly states that all prime ideals in 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G are virtually standard. This is now known for large classes of prime ideals in various groups, but in general it remains open.

To simplify the conjecture, fix a prime ideal PP of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G and set

P†=ker⁡(G→𝒪​G×→(𝒪​G/P)×),P^{\dagger}=\ker(G\to\mathcal{O}G^{\times}\to(\mathcal{O}G/P)^{\times}),

a closed normal subgroup of GG: then PP contains the augmentation ideal ε=(P†−1)​𝒪​G\varepsilon=(P^{\dagger}-1)\mathcal{O}G, so we can pass to the quotient

P∗=P/ε⊆𝒪​G/ε≅𝒪​G∗,P^{*}=P/\varepsilon\subseteq\mathcal{O}G/\varepsilon\cong\mathcal{O}G^{*},

where G∗=G/P†G^{*}=G/P^{\dagger}. Then P∗P^{*} is a prime ideal of 𝒪​G∗\mathcal{O}G^{*}, and now we have (P∗)†=1(P^{*})^{\dagger}=1, so to prove PP is standard, we only need to prove that P∗P^{*} is centrally generated.

Note: The resulting group G∗G^{*} may no longer be pp-valuable, as it may no longer be torsion-free. However, there is a finite normal subgroup F∗≤G∗F^{*}\leq G^{*} such that the quotient G∗/F∗G^{*}/F^{*} is pp-valuable, and P∗∩𝒪​F∗P^{*}\cap\mathcal{O}F^{*} is the intersection of a GG-orbit of prime ideals of 𝒪​F∗≅𝒪⁡[F∗]\mathcal{O}F^{*}\cong\mathcal{O}[F^{*}], the (ordinary) group algebra of F∗F^{*}. Hence it is considered relatively harmless to assume that F∗=1F^{*}=1, or equivalently to assume without loss of generality from the start that P†=1P^{\dagger}=1.

We say that a prime ideal PP of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G is faithful if P†=1P^{\dagger}=1. Then setting Z=Z⁡(G)Z=Z(G) as the centre of GG, then our main conjecture can be restated as follows.

Conjecture A. If PP is a faithful prime ideal of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G, then P=(P∩𝒪​Z)​𝒪​GP=(P\cap\mathcal{O}Z)\mathcal{O}G.

There are two natural cases to consider here.

  1. 1.

    If π∈P\pi\in P, we may quotient out by (π)(\pi) and pass to k​G:=k⁡[[G]]≅𝒪​G/(π)kG:=k[[G]]\cong\mathcal{O}G/(\pi). This version of Conjecture A was asked as [1, Question O], and has since been proven true for GG nilpotent [4, Theorem 8.4], and for GG of the form ℤpd⋊ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{d}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{p} [7, Theorem 1.4].

  2. 2.

    If π∉P\pi\not\in P, we may invert π\pi and pass to K​G:=K⊗𝒪𝒪​G=𝒪​G​[1π]KG:=K\otimes_{\mathcal{O}}\mathcal{O}G=\mathcal{O}G[\frac{1}{\pi}]. Conjecture A is known for prime ideals of infinite codimension when GG is semisimple of type AA or DD [12, Theorem 3], [11, Theorem 2], or for primitive ideals when GG is nilpotent [9, Theorem A].

(Warning: K​GKG is not the same as K⁡[[G]]K[[G]]. For example, if we take ℤp​[[x]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[[x]] and invert pp, we do not get ℚp​[[x]]\mathbb{Q}_{p}[[x]].)

In this paper, we restrict to case 2, about which much less is known. We will also assume that GG is a nilpotent group, and we want to build on the results from [9] and try to prove Conjecture A for all prime ideals, rather than just primitive ones.

In §3, we will recall a certain characteristic abelian subgroup A⁡(G)A(G) of GG, originally constructed in [9, §3.5], containing the centre ZZ. When approaching the conjecture for general prime results, the strongest result to date is:

Theorem. [9, Theorem B] Setting A:=A⁡(G)A:=A(G), if PP is a faithful prime ideal of K​GKG, then P=(P∩K​A)​K​GP=(P\cap KA)KG.

Of course, if A⁡(G)=ZA(G)=Z, then Conjecture A follows immediately from this theorem. There are cases when this is true, for example when GG has nilpotency class 2, but it is sadly false in the vast majority of cases of interest. Indeed, whenever the second centre Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is abelian (which is the case for all nilpotent groups arising as positive root subgroups) then A⁡(G)A(G) is strictly larger than the centre.

Moreover, the construction of A⁡(G)A(G) relies on an iterative procedure (which can be of arbitrary finite length), and so it can be time-consuming to compute.

In this note, we will define a smaller subgroup B⁡(G)B(G) of GG, with Z⊆B⁡(G)⊆A⁡(G)Z\subseteq B(G)\subseteq A(G). This subgroup is much more explicitly constructed, and can often be computed more easily. Our main result is very similar:

Theorem 1. (Theorem 3.10) Setting B:=B⁡(G)B:=B(G), if PP is a faithful prime ideal of K​GKG, then P=(P∩K​B)​K​GP=(P\cap KB)KG.∎

Needless to say, how much of an improvement this result is depends entirely on how much smaller than A⁡(G)A(G) the subgroup B⁡(G)B(G) actually is. There are several cases when B⁡(G)=A⁡(G)B(G)=A(G) (including of course all the cases when A⁡(G)=ZA(G)=Z), so this result constitutes no improvement in this setting.

However, in §4, we will explore a number of examples of groups GG for which we can prove that B⁡(G)B(G) is a proper subgroup of A⁡(G)A(G), and in several of them we even have that B⁡(G)=ZB(G)=Z. Using our main theorem this is enough to prove Conjecture A for these groups, and in particular for the majority of those groups that arise from Lie theory:

Theorem 2. (Corollary 4.9) If GG is nilpotent and Lie(G)(G) is the positive root subalgebra of a split-semisimple ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-Lie algebra, containing no component of type CC. Then for any faithful prime ideal PP of K​GKG, (P∩K​Z)​K​G=P(P\cap KZ)KG=P.

It is curious that this approach fails when GG is a positive root subgroup of type CC, though we still believe the conjecture to be true in this case.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we will recap some of the key concepts we will be using throughout the article. Firstly, with regard to notation, if gg and hh are elements of a group, we will write gh=h​g​h−1{}^{h}g=hgh^{-1}. To distinguish between group commutators and ring commutators, we will write the former as (g,h)=gh⋅h−1=g−1h−1gh(g,h)={\vphantom{h}}^{g}h\cdot h^{-1}=g^{-1}h^{-1}gh and the latter as [x,y]=x​y−y​x[x,y]=xy-yx throughout this paper.

The following facts about group commutators are well known, and can be easily checked directly: we include them only for ease of reference later.

Lemma 2.1.

Let GG be a group, nn any positive integer, and a,b,c∈Ga,b,c\in G arbitrary elements.

  1. (i)

    (ab,c)=(b,c)a⋅(a,c)(ab,c)={}^{a}(b,c)\cdot(a,c).

  2. (ii)

    (an,c)=(a,c)an−1⋅(a,c)an−2…(a,c)a⋅(a,c)(a^{n},c)={}^{a^{n-1}}(a,c)\cdot{}^{a^{n-2}}(a,c)\dots{}^{a}(a,c)\cdot(a,c).∎

2.1 pp-valuable groups

Definition 2.2.

[10, Ch. III, Définition 2.1.2] A pp-valuation ω\omega on a group GG is a function ω:G→ℝ∪{∞}\omega:G\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} such that, for all g,h∈Gg,h\in G,

  1. (i)

    ω⁡(g​h−1)≥min⁡{ω⁡(g),ω⁡(h)}\omega(gh^{-1})\geq\min\{\omega(g),\omega(h)\},

  2. (ii)

    ω⁡((g,h))≥ω⁡(g)+ω⁡(h)\omega((g,h))\geq\omega(g)+\omega(h),

  3. (iii)

    ω⁡(gp)=ω⁡(g)+1\omega(g^{p})=\omega(g)+1,

  4. (iv)

    ω⁡(g)>(p−1)−1\omega(g)>(p-1)^{-1}, and

  5. (v)

    ω⁡(g)=∞⇔g=1\omega(g)=\infty\Leftrightarrow g=1.

Moreover, we say that the pp-valuation ω\omega is saturated if for all g∈Gg\in G such that ω⁡(g)>1p−1+1\omega(g)>\frac{1}{p-1}+1, there exists h∈Gh\in G with g=hpg=h^{p}.

Note: If GG carries a pp-valuation then it is torsionfree, and if gp=hpg^{p}=h^{p} for any g,h∈Gg,h\in G then g=hg=h. In particular, if ω\omega is saturated and ω⁡(g)>1p−1+1\omega(g)>\frac{1}{p-1}+1, then there is a unique element hh such that hp=gh^{p}=g, we write h=gp−1h=g^{p^{-1}}.

Defined in this way, a pp-valuation is a kind of group filtration. More precisely, we isolate the following properties from [10].

Properties 2.3.

Let GG be a group and ω\omega a fixed pp-valuation on GG.

  1. 1.

    Given any ν∈ℝ\nu\in\mathbb{R}, write Gν=ω−1​([ν,∞])G_{\nu}=\omega^{-1}([\nu,\infty]) and Gν+=ω−1​((ν,∞])G_{\nu^{+}}=\omega^{-1}((\nu,\infty]). These are normal subgroups of GG, and the quotient group grν​(G)=Gν/Gν+\mathrm{gr}_{\nu}(G)=G_{\nu}/G_{\nu^{+}} is abelian, so we will write its group operation as addition.

  2. 2.

    Define the associated graded group gr⁡(G)=⨁ν∈ℝgrν​(G)\displaystyle\mathrm{gr}(G)=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{gr}_{\nu}(G) [10, Ch. II, 1.1.7.2]. It follows from Definition 2.2(iii) that gr⁡(G)\mathrm{gr}(G) is an 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-module, and any non-identity element g∈Gg\in G gives a nonzero homogeneous element gr⁡(g):=g+Gμ+∈grμ​(G)\mathrm{gr}(g):=g+G_{\mu^{+}}\in\mathrm{gr}_{\mu}(G), where μ=ω⁡(g)\mu=\omega(g). Moreover, if ω⁡(g)=μ\omega(g)=\mu and ω⁡(h)=ν\omega(h)=\nu, we may define a bracket operation on gr⁡(G)\mathrm{gr}(G):

    [gr⁡(g),gr⁡(h)]:=(g,h)+G(μ+ν)+,[\mathrm{gr}(g),\mathrm{gr}(h)]:=(g,h)+G_{(\mu+\nu)^{+}},

    which extends bilinearly to an 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-Lie algebra structure on gr⁡(G)\mathrm{gr}(G) [10, Ch. II, 1.1.7].

  3. 3.

    There is also an 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-linear endomorphism π:gr⁡(G)→gr⁡(G)\pi:\mathrm{gr}(G)\to\mathrm{gr}(G), uniquely defined by its action π⁡(gr⁡(g))=gr⁡(gp)\pi(\mathrm{gr}(g))=\mathrm{gr}(g^{p}) on homogeneous elements. This makes gr⁡(G)\mathrm{gr}(G) into an 𝔽p​[π]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\pi]-Lie algebra [10, Ch. II, 2.1.1] which is torsion-free [10, Ch. I, Théorème 1.2.3], and we will say that the rank of GG is the rank of gr⁡(G)\mathrm{gr}(G) as a 𝔽p​[π]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\pi]-module [10, Définition 2.1.3].

  4. 4.

    There is also a notion of completion [10, Ch. II, 1.1.5]: set G^=lim←ν∈ℝ⁡G/Gν\displaystyle\widehat{G}=\varprojlim_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}G/G_{\nu}, and say that GG is complete (with respect to ω\omega) if the natural map G→G^G\to\widehat{G} is an isomorphism. Equivalently, we could define a metric on GG by d⁡(g,h):=ω⁡(g−1​h)d(g,h):=\omega(g^{-1}h), and GG is complete if and only if it is topologically complete with respect to this metric.

Note: If GG is complete with respect to ω\omega then for any pp-adic integer λ\lambda, if we write λ:=∑n∈ℕ​λn​pn\lambda:=\underset{n\in\mathbb{N}}{\sum}\lambda_{n}p^{n} with 0≤λn<p0\leq\lambda_{n}<p, then we can define gλg^{\lambda} for any g∈Gg\in G to be the limit of the sequence ∏n=1𝑁​gλn​pn\overset{N}{\underset{n=1}{\prod}}g^{\lambda_{n}p^{n}} as N→∞N\rightarrow\infty.

Definition 2.4.

[4, Definition 4.5] Let GG be a group and ω\omega a fixed pp-valuation. The degree of an automorphism φ\varphi of GG (with respect to ω\omega) is

deg⁡(φ)=degω⁡(φ)=infg∈G{ω⁡(φ⁡(g)​g−1)−ω⁡(g)}.\deg(\varphi)=\deg_{\omega}(\varphi)=\inf_{g\in G}\left\{\omega(\varphi(g)g^{-1})-\omega(g)\right\}.

We will say that φ\varphi is bounded if deg⁡(φ)>(p−1)−1\deg(\varphi)>(p-1)^{-1}.

Note that, if φ\varphi is conjugation by some fixed h∈Gh\in G, then by Definition 2.2(ii), (iv), φ\varphi is bounded with respect to any pp-valuation ω\omega. So, following Lazard, we now make the following definition:

Definition 2.5.

[10, Ch. III, Definition 3.1.6] A group GG is pp-valuable if there exists a pp-valuation ω\omega with respect to which GG is complete and has finite rank. Moreover, we say that GG is pp-saturable if ω\omega is saturated.

Example 2.6.

We say GG is a uniform pro-pp group if it a finitely generated, torsionfree pro-pp group, and (G,G)⊆Gp(G,G)\subseteq G^{p} [6, Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.5]. In this case, we can define a pp-valuation ω\omega on GG by

ω⁡(g):=sup{n∈ℕ:g∈Gpn}\omega(g):=\sup\{n\in\mathbb{N}:g\in G^{p^{n}}\}

With respect to ω\omega, GG is a pp-valuable, and in fact pp-saturable group.

Proposition 2.7.

[10, III.3.3] For every pp-valuable group GG, there exists a canonical pp-saturable group S​a​t​(G)Sat(G) such that GG can be embedded as an open normal subgroup of S​a​t​(G)Sat(G).

2.2 Lazard’s equivalence of categories

Let GG be a pp-valuable group, with pp-valuation ω\omega, and let ΛG:=ℤp​G\Lambda_{G}:=\mathbb{Z}_{p}G be the ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Iwasawa algebra of GG. Then ΛG\Lambda_{G} carries a natural topology inherited from ω\omega. Specifically, we know using [10, III.2.3.6] that there exists a separated ring filtration ww on the group algebra ℤp​[G]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[G] such that

  • •

    ww restricts to the pp-adic valuation vpv_{p} on ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p},

  • •

    w⁡(g−1)>1w(g-1)>1 for all g∈Gg\in G,

  • •

    the associated graded ring grw​ℤp​[G]\mathrm{gr}_{w}\mathbb{Z}_{p}[G] is isomorphic to the enveloping algebra of the Lie algebra grω​(G)\mathrm{gr}_{\omega}(G), and

  • •

    ΛG\Lambda_{G} arises as the topological completion of ℤp​[G]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[G] with respect to ww.

Therefore, we can of course extend ww to ΛG\Lambda_{G}. Moreover, ww extends further to the rational Iwasawa algebra ℚp​G=ℚp⊗ℤpΛG\mathbb{Q}_{p}G=\mathbb{Q}_{p}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\Lambda_{G}, where we define w⁡(p−m⊗r):=w⁡(r)−mw(p^{-m}\otimes r):=w(r)-m. However, ℚp​G\mathbb{Q}_{p}G is no longer complete with respect to ww, so we can pass to the completion ℚp​G^\widehat{\mathbb{Q}_{p}G} of ℚp​G\mathbb{Q}_{p}G with respect to ww.

Now, inside ΛG\Lambda_{G}, w⁡(g−1)>1w(g-1)>1, so w⁡((g−1)n)≥n≥vp​(n)=w⁡(n)w((g-1)^{n})\geq n\geq v_{p}(n)=w(n), so it follows that the sequence ((−1)n+1n​(g−1)n)\left(\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}(g-1)^{n}\right) converges to 0 in ℚp​G\mathbb{Q}_{p}G, and hence the logarithm series log⁡(g):=∑n∈ℕ​(−1)n+1n​(g−1)n\log(g):=\underset{n\in\mathbb{N}}{\sum}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}(g-1)^{n} converges in ℚp​G^\widehat{\mathbb{Q}_{p}G}.

Now, if ω\omega is a saturated pp-valuation, we define the ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie lattice of GG to be the set

log⁡(G):={log⁡(g):g∈G}⊆ℚp​G^\log(G):=\{\log(g):g\in G\}\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb{Q}_{p}G}
Theorem 2.8.

[10, IV.3.2.3]

For any pp-saturable group GG, log⁡(G)\log(G) is a free ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie subalgebra of ℚp​G^\widehat{\mathbb{Q}_{p}G} of finite rank, equal to the rank of GG. Moreover, for any g,h∈Gg,h\in G, λ∈ℤp\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}:

  • •

    λ​log⁡(g)=log⁡(gλ)\lambda\log(g)=\log(g^{\lambda})

  • •

    log⁡(g)+log⁡(h)=log⁡(limn→∞​(gpn​hpn)p−n)\log(g)+\log(h)=\log\left(\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim}{\left(g^{p^{n}}h^{p^{n}}\right)^{p^{-n}}}\right)

  • •

    [log⁡(g),log⁡(h)]=log⁡(limn→∞​(gpn,hpn)p−2​n)[\log(g),\log(h)]=\log\left(\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim}{\left(g^{p^{n}},h^{p^{n}}\right)^{p^{-2n}}}\right)

In fact, the functor G↦log⁡(G)G\mapsto\log(G) defines an equivalence (and in fact isomorphism) of categories between the category of pp-saturable groups and a certain category of free ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie algebras known as saturable Lie algebras [10, IV.3.2.6]. This is known as Lazard’s equivalence of categories.

Example 2.9.

If GG is a uniform pro-pp group, then if we let ℒ:=log⁡(G)\mathcal{L}:=\log(G), then ℒ\mathcal{L} is a powerful ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie algebra, i.e. [ℒ,ℒ]⊆p​ℒ[\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L}]\subseteq p\mathcal{L}.

Moreover, the logarithm functor restricts to an equivalence of categories between the category of uniform pro-pp groups and the category of powerful ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie algebras of finite rank.

Lazard’s equivalence will prove useful when looking for examples of pp-valuable groups, since it is practically much easier to start with a powerful ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie algebra and pass to its image under the inverse functor exp\exp rather than look for examples directly.

Finally, we define the Lie algebra of a pp-valuable group GG to be the ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-Lie algebra

𝔤G=L​i​e​(G):=ℚp⊗ℤplog⁡(S​a​t​(G))\mathfrak{g}_{G}=Lie(G):=\mathbb{Q}_{p}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\log(Sat(G))

Unfortunately, the functor G→𝔤GG\to\mathfrak{g}_{G} is no kind of equivalence of categories, and there are plenty of examples of non-isomorphic groups G,HG,H such that 𝔤G=𝔤H\mathfrak{g}_{G}=\mathfrak{g}_{H} (for example, if HH is any open subgroup of GG). But note that whenever GG is pp-saturable, log⁡(G)\log(G) is a full rank ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-Lie lattice in 𝔤G\mathfrak{g}_{G}.

Remark 2.10.

If GG is not pp-saturable, then log⁡(G)⊆ℚp​G^\log(G)\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb{Q}_{p}G} need not be closed under addition or the Lie bracket. Still, we can embed log⁡(G)\log(G) as a subset of log⁡(S​a​t​(G))\log(Sat(G)), so it will still span 𝔤G\mathfrak{g}_{G} as a ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-vector space.

Lemma 2.11.

For any pp-valuable group GG, the map H↦𝔤HH\mapsto\mathfrak{g}_{H} defines an inclusion preserving bijection between the set of closed, isolated normal subgroups of GG and the set of ideals of 𝔤G\mathfrak{g}_{G}.∎

2.3 Right ideals and controlling subgroups

Let GG be a pp-valuable group and let II be a right ideal of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G (or K​GKG). We say that a subgroup HH of GG controls II if II is generated by a subset of 𝒪​H\mathcal{O}H (or K​HKH), i.e. I=(I∩𝒪​H)​𝒪​GI=(I\cap\mathcal{O}H)\mathcal{O}G (or I=(I∩K​H)​K​GI=(I\cap KH)KG).

Lemma 2.12.

There exist mutually inverse bijections

where Φ⁡(Q):=K⊗𝒪Q\Phi(Q):=K\otimes_{\mathcal{O}}Q and Ψ⁡(P):=P∩𝒪​G\Psi(P):=P\cap\mathcal{O}G. Moreover, Φ​(Q)†=Q†\Phi(Q)^{\dagger}=Q^{\dagger}, and PP is controlled by a closed, normal subgroup HH of GG if and only if Φ⁡(P)\Phi(P) is controlled by HH.

Proof.

It is straightforward to show that every two-sided ideal II of K​GKG can be written as K⊗𝒪JK\otimes_{\mathcal{O}}J, where J=I∩𝒪​GJ=I\cap\mathcal{O}G, and that II is prime if and only if JJ is prime.

On the other hand, if QQ is a prime ideal of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G not containing pp, then let P:=K⊗𝒪QP:=K\otimes_{\mathcal{O}}Q. It is clear that Q⊆P∩𝒪​GQ\subseteq P\cap\mathcal{O}G, and for all r∈P∩𝒪​Gr\in P\cap\mathcal{O}G, there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that pn​r∈Qp^{n}r\in Q. But pp is central in 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G, so since p∉Qp\notin Q and QQ is prime, it follows that r∈Qr\in Q. Therefore P∩𝒪​G=QP\cap\mathcal{O}G=Q, so it follows that Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi are well defined, mutually inverse bijections.

Moreover, for all group elements g∈Gg\in G, and all prime ideals PP of K​GKG, since g−1∈ℤ⁡[G]⊆𝒪​Gg-1\in\mathbb{Z}[G]\subseteq\mathcal{O}G, it follows that g−1∈Pg-1\in P if and only if g−1∈P∩𝒪​G=Ψ⁡(P)g-1\in P\cap\mathcal{O}G=\Psi(P), so P†=Ψ​(P)†P^{\dagger}=\Psi(P)^{\dagger}. Since Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi are mutually inverse, it follows immediately that Φ​(Q)†=Q†\Phi(Q)^{\dagger}=Q^{\dagger} for all prime ideals QQ of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G not containing pp.

Now, if HH controls a prime ideal QQ of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G with p∉Qp\notin Q, then for any r∈Φ⁡(Q)r\in\Phi(Q), we know that pn​r∈Qp^{n}r\in Q for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, so we can write pn​r=s1​r1+⋯+sk​rkp^{n}r=s_{1}r_{1}+\dots+s_{k}r_{k} for some si∈Q∩𝒪​Hs_{i}\in Q\cap\mathcal{O}H, ri∈𝒪​Gr_{i}\in\mathcal{O}G. Thus r=p−n⊗(s1​r1+⋯+sk​rk)=(p−n⊗s1)​r1+⋯+(p−n⊗sk)​rkr=p^{-n}\otimes(s_{1}r_{1}+\dots+s_{k}r_{k})=(p^{-n}\otimes s_{1})r_{1}+\dots+(p^{-n}\otimes s_{k})r_{k}, and since p−n⊗si∈K⊗(Q∩𝒪​H)=P∩K​Hp^{-n}\otimes s_{i}\in K\otimes(Q\cap\mathcal{O}H)=P\cap KH, it follows that HH controls PP.

Finally, let PP be a prime ideal of K​GKG, and it remains to prove that if HH controls PP then HH controls Q:=Φ⁡(P)=P∩𝒪​GQ:=\Phi(P)=P\cap\mathcal{O}G.

Using [5, Theorem A], we know that HH controls QQ if and only if QQ is controlled by any open normal subgroup of GG containing HH. Since PP is also controlled by any such open normal subgroup, we may assume that HH is open in GG, so let {g1,…,gk}\{g_{1},\dots,g_{k}\} be a complete set of coset representatives for HH in GG.

If r∈Qr\in Q then we can write r=∑1≤i≤k​ri​gir=\underset{1\leq i\leq k}{\sum}r_{i}g_{i} for some ri∈𝒪​Hr_{i}\in\mathcal{O}H. But r∈P=(P∩K​H)​K​Gr\in P=(P\cap KH)KG, so we know that ri∈P∩K​Hr_{i}\in P\cap KH for each i≤ki\leq k, thus ri∈P∩K​H∩𝒪​G=P∩𝒪​H=Q∩𝒪​Hr_{i}\in P\cap KH\cap\mathcal{O}G=P\cap\mathcal{O}H=Q\cap\mathcal{O}H. So r∈(Q∩𝒪​H)​𝒪​Gr\in(Q\cap\mathcal{O}H)\mathcal{O}G, and QQ is controlled by HH as required.∎

If II is a right ideal of K​GKG, we define the controller subgroup IχI^{\chi} of II to be the intersection of all open subgroups UU of GG controlling II, which is of course a closed subgroup of GG.

Lemma 2.13.

If PP is a prime ideal of K​GKG, then PχP^{\chi} is a closed, normal subgroup of GG, and a subgroup HH of GG controls PP if and only if Pχ⊆HP^{\chi}\subseteq H. In particular, PχP^{\chi} controls PP.

Proof.

Clearly PχP^{\chi} is a closed subgroup of GG, and if an open subgroup UU of GG controls PP then for all g∈Gg\in G, (P∩Kg​U)​K​G=g⁡(P∩K​U)​K​G​g−1=g​P​g−1=P(P\cap K^{g}U)KG=g(P\cap KU)KGg^{-1}=gPg^{-1}=P, so Ug{}^{g}U controls PP. It follows that the intersection PχP^{\chi} of all open subgroups controlling PP is a normal subgroup of GG.

Now, using Lemma 2.12, we can write P=K⊗𝒪QP=K\otimes_{\mathcal{O}}Q, where Q=P∩𝒪​GQ=P\cap\mathcal{O}G is a prime ideal of 𝒪​G\mathcal{O}G, and a closed subgroup of GG controls PP if and only if it controls QQ, and hence Pχ=QχP^{\chi}=Q^{\chi}. But by [5, Theorem A], a closed subgroup of GG controls QQ if and only if it contains Qχ=PχQ^{\chi}=P^{\chi} as required.∎

Definition 2.14.

  1. (i)

    [4, Definition 5.5] A prime ideal PP of K​GKG is non-splitting if P∩K​HP\cap KH is prime for any open normal subgroup H⊲GH\lhd G that controls PP.

  2. (ii)

    [4, Definition 5.7] A right ideal II of K​GKG is virtually non-splitting if I=P​K​GI=PKG for some non-splitting prime ideal P⊲K​HP\lhd KH and some open subgroup H≤GH\leq G.

Properties 2.15.

  1. (i)

    [8, Proposition 4.3] If PP is non-splitting, then P∩K​PχP\cap KP^{\chi} is prime.

  2. (ii)

    [9, Theorem 3.17] Let CC be a closed subgroup of GG. If all faithful virtually non-splitting right ideals of K​GKG are controlled by CC, then all faithful prime ideals of K​GKG are controlled by CC.

Here is our first refinement:

Proposition 2.16.

Let GG be a nontrivial pp-valuable group, and suppose that for every normal subgroup UU of GG, every faithful prime ideal of K​UKU is controlled by Z2​(U)Z_{2}(U). Then every faithful prime PP of K​GKG is controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).

Proof.

First, suppose PP is non-splitting, so that Q:=P∩K​PχQ:=P\cap KP^{\chi} is a faithful prime ideal of K​PχKP^{\chi}, and Qχ=PχQ^{\chi}=P^{\chi}. Fix g∈G∖Zg\in G\setminus Z, and let φg\varphi_{g} be the bounded automorphism of GG given by conjugation by gg. Clearly φg​(Q)=Q\varphi_{g}(Q)=Q, and φ\varphi centralises both ZZ and Qχ/ZQ^{\chi}/Z, but QQ is not controlled by any proper open subgroup of QχQ^{\chi}, so by Theorem 2.17 φg\varphi_{g} must act trivially on QχQ^{\chi}. But since gg was arbitrary, this says that every g∈Gg\in G centralises QχQ^{\chi}, i.e. Qχ⊆ZQ^{\chi}\subseteq Z.

Now suppose I=P​K​GI=PKG is a faithful virtually non-splitting right ideal, for PP a faithful prime ideal in K​UKU, for UU an open normal subgroup of GG. Then PP is controlled by Z2​(U)Z_{2}(U) by assumption, so using the argument above we see that PP is controlled by Z⁡(U)=Z⁡(G)∩UZ(U)=Z(G)\cap U, so

(I∩K​Z​(G))​K​G=(P∩K​Z​(U))​K​U⋅K​G=P​K​G=I(I\cap KZ(G))KG=(P\cap KZ(U))KU\cdot KG=PKG=I

It follows from Properties 2.15 that all faithful prime ideals in K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).∎

The basic control theorem we will use throughout this note is:

Theorem 2.17.

[9, Theorem 3.16] Let GG be a pp-valuable group and let PP be a faithful prime ideal of K​GKG such that K​G/PKG/P is infinite dimensional over KK. Fix a nontrivial bounded automorphism φ\varphi of GG and a closed central subgroup 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of GG.

If φ⁡(P)=P\varphi(P)=P, and φ\varphi centralises both 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and G/𝒵G/\mathcal{Z}, then PP is controlled by a proper open subgroup of GG.∎

The requirement that PP have infinite codimension in K​GKG may seem problematic, but we are principally interested in the case where GG is solvable, in which case this does not pose a problem:

Proposition 2.18.

If GG is a non-abelian, solvable pp-valuable group and PP is a faithful prime ideal of K​GKG, then K​G/PKG/P is infinite dimensional over KK

Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that PP is faithful and K​G/PKG/P is finite dimensional. Since it is also a prime ring, there must exist a finite dimensional, irreducible K​GKG-module MM such that P=A​n​nK​G​MP=Ann_{KG}M.

The action of K​GKG on MM extends to the completion K​G^\widehat{KG}, which contains the Lie algebra log⁡(G)\log(G) of GG as a subalgebra. This Lie algebra is solvable, so by Lie’s theorem there must exist a finite extension of fields F/KF/K such that F⊗KMF\otimes_{K}M is completely solvable over log⁡(G)\log(G). In particular, F⊗KMF\otimes_{K}M contains a submodule NN of codimension 1, so let M′:=(F⊗KM)/NM^{\prime}:=(F\otimes_{K}M)/N.

Now, the action of K​GKG on MM extends to an action of F​GFG on F⊗KMF\otimes_{K}M, and NN remains an F​GFG-submodule. So M′M^{\prime} is a F​GFG-module, and the natural map M→M′M\to M^{\prime} is a non-zero K​GKG-module map. Moreover, since MM is irreducible as a K​GKG-module, this map must be injective, so setting Q:=A​n​nF​G​M′Q:=Ann_{FG}M^{\prime} we see that Q∩K​G=A​n​nK​G​M′⊆A​n​nK​G​M=PQ\cap KG=Ann_{KG}M^{\prime}\subseteq Ann_{KG}M=P.

But M′M^{\prime} is one dimensional over FF, so writing M′=F​vM^{\prime}=Fv, there exists a Lie algebra homomorphism λ:log⁡(G)→F\lambda:\log(G)\to F such that x⋅v=λ⁡(x)​vx\cdot v=\lambda(x)v for all x∈log⁡(G)x\in\log(G). Let 𝔥:=ker⁡(λ)\mathfrak{h}:=\ker(\lambda); an ideal of log⁡(G)\log(G) acting by zero on M′M^{\prime}, and since log⁡(G)\log(G) is non-abelian, 𝔥≠0\mathfrak{h}\neq 0. Let H:=exp⁡(𝔥)H:=\exp(\mathfrak{h}); a non-trivial normal subgroup of GG, acting by the identity on M′M^{\prime}, and hence (H−1)​K​G⊆Q∩K​G⊆P(H-1)KG\subseteq Q\cap KG\subseteq P, contradicting faithfulness.

Thus we conclude that PP has infinite codimension in K​GKG.∎

3 Control theorems

Throughout this section, we will fix GG a pp-valuable group.

Definition 3.1.

  • •

    The lower central series of GG is the chain of closed, isolated, characteristic subgroups: 1=Z0​(G)⊆Z1​(G)⊆Z2​(G)⊆…1=Z_{0}(G)\subseteq Z_{1}(G)\subseteq Z_{2}(G)\subseteq\dots, where for all i>0i>0,

    Zi​(G):={g∈G:(g,G)⊆Zi−1​(G)}Z_{i}(G):=\{g\in G:(g,G)\subseteq Z_{i-1}(G)\}
  • •

    If HH is a subgroup of GG, define the centraliser of HH to be the subgroup

    𝐂G​(H):={g∈G:(g,H)=1}\mathbf{C}_{G}(H):=\{g\in G:(g,H)=1\}

    Note that if HH is closed/isolated/characteristic then so is CG​(H)C_{G}(H).

3.1 Old Control Theorem: The subgroup A⁡(G)A(G)

In [9, section 3], the first author applied Theorem 2.17 to prove a control theorem for faithful prime ideals in K​GKG, which we will recap in full detail now.

Definition 3.2.

Define a descending sequence of subgroups G=A0⊇A1⊇A2⊇…G=A_{0}\supseteq A_{1}\supseteq A_{2}\supseteq\dots by Ai+1:=𝐂Ai​(Z2​(Ai))A_{i+1}:=\mathbf{C}_{A_{i}}(Z_{2}(A_{i})). Set A⁡(G):=⋂i∈ℕAiA(G):=\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb{N}}A_{i}.

Note that each AiA_{i} is a closed, isolated, characteristic subgroup of GG, so it follows that the sequence G=A0⊇A1⊇…G=A_{0}\supseteq A_{1}\supseteq\dots must terminate, and thus A⁡(G)=AnA(G)=A_{n} for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}.

Lemma 3.3.

A⁡(G)A(G) is a proper subgroup of GG if and only if Z​(G)≠Z2​(G)Z(G)\neq Z_{2}(G), and if GG is nilpotent then A⁡(G)A(G) is abelian.

Proof.

Since A1=𝐂G​(Z2​(G))A_{1}=\mathbf{C}_{G}(Z_{2}(G)), it is clear that this is a proper subgroup of GG if and only if Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is not central in GG, i.e. if and only if Z​(G)≠Z2​(G)Z(G)\neq Z_{2}(G).

If GG is nilpotent, then for each i≥0i\geq 0, AiA_{i} is nilpotent, so either AiA_{i} is abelian or Z⁡(Ai)≠Z2​(Ai)Z(A_{i})\neq Z_{2}(A_{i}). In the latter case, Ai+1=𝐂Ai​(Z2​(Ai))A_{i+1}=\mathbf{C}_{A_{i}}(Z_{2}(A_{i})) is a proper subgroup of AiA_{i}. Therefore, either AiA_{i} is abelian for some ii, or the descending sequence G=A0⊇A1⊇…G=A_{0}\supseteq A_{1}\supseteq\dots does not terminate. But we know this sequence does terminate at A⁡(G)A(G), so this implies that AiA_{i} is abelian for sufficiently high ii, and hence A⁡(G)A(G) is abelian.∎

The following result is a direct application of Theorem 2.17.

Theorem 3.4.

[9, Theorem B and proof in §3.5] If GG is solvable and PP is a faithful prime ideal of K​GKG, then PP is controlled by A⁡(G)A(G).∎

Note: The statement of [9, Theorem B] required GG to be nilpotent, but since we know that all prime ideals in K​GKG have infinite codimension by Proposition 2.18, the proof goes through without issue.

Corollary 3.5.

If Z2​(G)=GZ_{2}(G)=G then all faithful prime ideals of K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).

Proof.

By definition, A1:=𝐂G​(Z2​(G))=𝐂G​(G)=Z⁡(G)A_{1}:=\mathbf{C}_{G}(Z_{2}(G))=\mathbf{C}_{G}(G)=Z(G), so for all i>1i>1,

Ai=𝐂Ai−1​(Z2​(Ai−1))=𝐂Z⁡(G)​(Z2​(Z⁡(G)))=Z⁡(G)A_{i}=\mathbf{C}_{A_{i-1}}(Z_{2}(A_{i-1}))=\mathbf{C}_{Z(G)}(Z_{2}(Z(G)))=Z(G)

hence A⁡(G)=Z⁡(G)A(G)=Z(G), so all faithful prime ideals of K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G) by Theorem 3.4.∎

Unfortunately, the condition that Z2​(G)=GZ_{2}(G)=G is very restrictive, but there are few other examples known where A⁡(G)=Z⁡(G)A(G)=Z(G). Indeed, the following result confirms that this is generally very false.

Lemma 3.6.

If Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is abelian and Z2​(G)≠Z​(G)Z_{2}(G)\neq Z(G), then Z2​(G)⊆A​(G)Z_{2}(G)\subseteq A(G) and A⁡(G)≠Z⁡(G)A(G)\neq Z(G).

Proof.

Since Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is abelian, Z2​(G)⊆A1=CG​(Z2​(G))Z_{2}(G)\subseteq A_{1}=C_{G}(Z_{2}(G)), and in fact Z2​(G)⊆Z⁡(A1)Z_{2}(G)\subseteq Z(A_{1}). For any i≥1i\geq 1, Z⁡(Ai)⊆CG​(Z2​(Ai))=Ai+1Z(A_{i})\subseteq C_{G}(Z_{2}(A_{i}))=A_{i+1}, and since Z⁡(Ai)Z(A_{i}) commutes with everything in Ai⊇Ai+1A_{i}\supseteq A_{i+1}, it follows that Z⁡(Ai)⊆Z⁡(Ai+1)Z(A_{i})\subseteq Z(A_{i+1}).

So suppose i≥1i\geq 1 and Z2​(G)⊆Z⁡(Ai)Z_{2}(G)\subseteq Z(A_{i}), then Z2​(G)⊆Z⁡(Ai+1)⊆AiZ_{2}(G)\subseteq Z(A_{i+1})\subseteq A_{i}. So we see by induction that Z2​(G)⊆AnZ_{2}(G)\subseteq A_{n} for all nn, and hence Z2​(G)⊆A​(G)Z_{2}(G)\subseteq A(G).∎

Since Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is abelian for many nilpotent groups of interest, we would like a stronger control theorem.

3.2 New Control Theorem: The subgroup B⁡(G)B(G)

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the set of all subgroups HH of GG which satisfy the following property:

For all ​g∈G:if ​(g,(g,H))=1​ then ​(g,H)=1.\text{For all }g\in G:\,\text{if }(g,(g,H))=1\text{ then }(g,H)=1. (∗*)

Lemma 3.7.

But since H1,H2∈𝒮H_{1},H_{2}\in\mathcal{S}, this implies that (g,H1)=(g,H2)=1(g,H_{1})=(g,H_{2})=1, and hence (g,H1​H2)=1(g,H_{1}H_{2})=1 by Lemma 2.1.∎

    Suppose g∈Gg\in G and (g,(g,H))=1(g,(g,H))=1. But we know that B⁡(G)⊆HB(G)\subseteq H, so (g,(g,B⁡(G))=1CLOSE(g,(g,B(G))=1, and hence (g,B⁡(G))=1(g,B(G))=1 by ( ∗ ‣ 3.2). III, 2.1.4], so that (g,h)=1(g,h)=1. Hence (g,H)=1(g,H)=1 and HH also satisfies ( ∗ ‣ 3.2). Thus we conclude that B⁡(G)⊆H⊆B⁡(G)B(G)\subseteq H\subseteq B(G), so B⁡(G)=HB(G)=H is isolated in GG.

Theorem 3.10.

⊆(P∩K​B​(U))​K​G\displaystyle\subseteq(P\cap KB(U))KG
⊆(I∩K​B​(U))​K​G,\displaystyle\subseteq(I\cap KB(U))KG,

But B⁡(U)⊆B⁡(G)B(U)\subseteq B(G) by Lemma 3.9, so it follows that II is controlled by B⁡(G)B(G). Applying Properties 2.15, we deduce that every faithful prime ideal of K​GKG is controlled by B⁡(G)B(G) as required.∎

3.3 Lie theoretic interpretation

For now, let 𝔤\mathfrak{g} be any finite dimensional ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-Lie algebra. Similar to the property ( ∗ ‣ 3.2) in §3.2, we define the following property of ideals 𝔞\mathfrak{a} of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}.

for all ​x∈𝔤:if ​[x,[x,𝔞]]=0​ then ​[x,𝔞]=0.\text{for all }x\in\mathfrak{g}:\,\text{if }[x,[x,\mathfrak{a}]]=0\text{ then }[x,\mathfrak{a}]=0. (∗⁣∗**)

Also similar to §3.2, we define B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}) to be the maximal ideal of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} satisfying ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3). It is very straightforward to prove that B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}) is uniquely defined, and that it contains Z⁡(𝔤)Z(\mathfrak{g}).

Now, fix a nilpotent pp-valuable group GG, and let 𝔤:=𝔤G\mathfrak{g}:=\mathfrak{g}_{G} be the Lie algebra of GG.

Proposition 3.11.

For any closed, isolated normal subgroup HH of GG, HH satisfies ( ∗ ‣ 3.2) if and only if 𝔥:=𝔤H\mathfrak{h}:=\mathfrak{g}_{H} satisfies ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3). In particular, B⁡(𝔤)=𝔤B⁡(G)B(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)}.

Proof.

We know by Lemma 2.11 that the map H↦𝔤HH\mapsto\mathfrak{g}_{H} is an inclusion preserving bijection between closed, isolated normal subgroups of GG and ideals in 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. Thus it suffices to prove the first statement, because since B⁡(G)B(G) is closed, isolated and normal in GG by Lemma 3.8, and all subgroups satisfying ( ∗ ‣ 3.2) are contained in B⁡(G)B(G), it will follow that 𝔤B⁡(G)\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)} satisfies ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3). Moreover, for any ideal 𝔥\mathfrak{h} satisfying ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3), 𝔥=𝔤H\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{g}_{H} for a normal subgroup HH satisfying ( ∗ ‣ 3.2), and hence H⊆B⁡(G)H\subseteq B(G) so 𝔥⊆𝔤B⁡(G)\mathfrak{h}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)}. In other words, 𝔤B⁡(G)=B⁡(𝔤)\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)}=B(\mathfrak{g}).

So, we want to prove that for any closed, isolated normal subgroup HH, HH satisfies ( ∗ ‣ 3.2) if and only if 𝔤H\mathfrak{g}_{H} satisfies ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3). Let us assume first that 𝔤H\mathfrak{g}_{H} satisfies ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3), and we are given g∈Gg\in G such that (g,(g,H))=1(g,(g,H))=1. Fixing any h∈Hh\in H, this means that gg commutes with (g,hpn)(g,h^{p^{n}}), and hence with (gpn,hpn)=(g,hpn)pn(g^{p^{n}},h^{p^{n}})=(g,h^{p^{n}})^{p^{n}} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} by Lemma 2.1. and gg must commute with (gpn,hpn)p−2​n∈S​a​t​(G)(g^{p^{n}},h^{p^{n}})^{p^{-2n}}\in Sat(G) for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Hence gg commutes with [log⁡(g),log⁡(h)][\log(g),\log(h)], so [log⁡(g),[log⁡(g),log⁡(h)]]=0[\log(g),[\log(g),\log(h)]]=0. Since this is true for all h∈Hh\in H, it follows that [log⁡(g),[log⁡(g),log⁡(H)]]=0[\log(g),[\log(g),\log(H)]]=0, and since 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is spanned by log⁡(H)\log(H), this means that [log⁡(g),[log⁡(g),𝔥]]=0[\log(g),[\log(g),\mathfrak{h}]]=0.

Conversely, if HH satisfies ( ∗ ‣ 3.2), then H⊆B⁡(G)⊆A⁡(G)H\subseteq B(G)\subseteq A(G) is abelian by Lemma 3.3. So set 𝔥:=𝔤H\mathfrak{h}:=\mathfrak{g}_{H}, and 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is an abelian ideal of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. Thus we conclude that (g,(g,h))=1(g,(g,h))=1 for all h∈Hh\in H, so applying ( ∗ ‣ 3.2) we deduce that (g,H)=1(g,H)=1. So since gg commutes with everything in HH, X:=log⁡(g)X:=\log(g) commutes with everything in log⁡(H)\log(H), and hence [x,log⁡(H)]=[p−n​X,log⁡(H)]=0[x,\log(H)]=[p^{-n}X,\log(H)]=0, so [x,𝔥]=0[x,\mathfrak{h}]=0 and 𝔥\mathfrak{h} satisfies ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3).∎

Moreover, since we know that Z⁡(𝔤)=𝔤Z⁡(G)Z(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{Z(G)}, we deduce the following useful consequence of Theorem 3.10.

Corollary 3.12.

If GG is a nilpotent pp-valuable group and B⁡(𝔤G)=Z⁡(𝔤G)B(\mathfrak{g}_{G})=Z(\mathfrak{g}_{G}), then all faithful prime ideals of K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).

Proof.

Setting 𝔤=𝔤G\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_{G}, we know that B⁡(𝔤)=𝔤B⁡(G)B(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)} by Proposition 3.11. But B⁡(G)B(G) is a closed, isolated normal subgroup of GG by Lemma 3.8, and so is Z⁡(G)Z(G). So since 𝔤Z⁡(G)=Z⁡(𝔤)=B⁡(𝔤)=𝔤B⁡(G)\mathfrak{g}_{Z(G)}=Z(\mathfrak{g})=B(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)} and the assignment H↦𝔤HH\mapsto\mathfrak{g}_{H} is injective for closed, isolated normal subgroups by Lemma 2.11, it follows that B⁡(G)=Z⁡(G)B(G)=Z(G). Using Theorem 3.10, we deduce that all faithful prime ideals of K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).∎

In §4 below, we will use the Lie algebra to calculate A⁡(G)A(G) and B⁡(G)B(G) explicitly for some pp-valuable nilpotent groups, and explore why this new control theorem is an improvement.

4 Examples

Throughout this section, we will fix 𝔤\mathfrak{g} a finite dimensional, nilpotent, ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-Lie algebra. We want to calculate B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}) for various examples.

4.1 Positive root bases

To first outline a possible method to calculating B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}), we want to focus on a particular class of examples.

Definition 4.1.

Given a basis {xi:i∈I}\{x_{i}:i\in I\} for 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, we say that this is a positive root basis if for every pair i,j∈Ii,j\in I, there exists k:=k⁡(i,j)∈Ik:=k(i,j)\in I such that [xi,xj]∈ℚp​xk[x_{i},x_{j}]\in\mathbb{Q}_{p}x_{k}.

Note: If [xi,xj]=0[x_{i},x_{j}]=0, we may take k⁡(i,j)k(i,j) to be any element of II. For convenience, we will usually take k⁡(i,j)=ik(i,j)=i in this case. If [xi,xj]≠0[x_{i},x_{j}]\neq 0 then k⁡(i,j)k(i,j) is uniquely defined.

Example 4.2.

The key examples of nilpotent Lie algebras carrying positive root bases come from Lie theory. Recall, if 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a split semisimple Lie algebra over ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, then the standard Cartan decomposition gives us

𝔰=𝔥⊕⨁α∈Φ​𝔰α\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{h}\oplus\underset{\alpha\in\Phi}{\bigoplus}\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha}

where 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is a Cartan subalgebra, Φ⊆𝔥∗\Phi\subseteq\mathfrak{h}^{\ast} is the root system of 𝔰\mathfrak{s}, and 𝔰α\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha} is the one dimensional α\alpha-eigenspace of the action of 𝔥\mathfrak{h} on 𝔰\mathfrak{s}. Note that for all α,β∈Φ\alpha,\beta\in\Phi,

[𝔰α,sβ]={𝔰α+βα+β∈Φ0otherwise[\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha},s_{\mathfrak{\beta}}]=\begin{cases}\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha+\beta}&\alpha+\beta\in\Phi\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

Decompose Φ=Φ+⊔Φ−\Phi=\Phi^{+}\sqcup\Phi^{-}, where Φ+\Phi^{+} (resp. Φ−\Phi^{-}) consist of the positive (resp. negative) roots in Φ\Phi with respect to some ordering, and let 𝔫+:=⨁α∈Φ+​𝔰α\mathfrak{n}^{+}:=\underset{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}}{\bigoplus}\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha} (resp. 𝔫−:=⨁α∈Φ−​𝔰α\mathfrak{n}^{-}:=\underset{\alpha\in\Phi^{-}}{\bigoplus}\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha}). Then 𝔫+,𝔫−\mathfrak{n}^{+},\mathfrak{n}^{-} are nilpotent subalgebras of 𝔰\mathfrak{s}, and we may write 𝔰=𝔫−⊕𝔥⊕𝔫+\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{n}^{-}\oplus\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{n}^{+}.

Let 𝔤:=𝔫+\mathfrak{g}:=\mathfrak{n}^{+}, and for each α∈Φ+\alpha\in\Phi^{+} let xαx_{\alpha} be a generator of the one dimensional space 𝔰α\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha}. Then {xα:α∈Φ+}\{x_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\} is a positive root basis for 𝔤\mathfrak{g} (hence the name), where the element k⁡(α,β)k(\alpha,\beta) from Definition 4.1 is defined by

k⁡(α,β)={α+βα+β∈Φαotherwisek(\alpha,\beta)=\begin{cases}\alpha+\beta&\alpha+\beta\in\Phi\\ \alpha&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

The following technical result provides a method of calculating B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}) whenever 𝔤\mathfrak{g} has a positive root basis.

Proposition 4.3.

Let {xi:i∈I}\{x_{i}:i\in I\} be a positive root basis for 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, and suppose B⁡(𝔤)⊆ Span​{xj:j∈J}B(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq\text{ Span}\{x_{j}:j\in J\} for some subset J⊆IJ\subseteq I. Suppose further that

  • •

    there exists i∈Ii\in I such that [xi,[xi,xj]]=0[x_{i},[x_{i},x_{j}]]=0 for all j∈Jj\in J.

  • •

    There exists a subset ∅≠S⊆J\varnothing\neq S\subseteq J, maximal with respect to the property that [xi,xm]≠0[x_{i},x_{m}]\neq 0 for all m∈Sm\in S.

  • •

    k⁡(i,m)≠k⁡(i,m′)k(i,m)\neq k(i,m^{\prime}) if m,m′∈Sm,m^{\prime}\in S and m≠m′m\neq m^{\prime}.

Then there exists a proper subset TT of JJ such that B⁡(𝔤)⊆ Span​{xj:j∈T}B(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq\text{ Span}\{x_{j}:j\in T\}.

Proof.

For each m∈Sm\in S, write [xi,xm]=μi,m​xk⁡(i,m)[x_{i},x_{m}]=\mu_{i,m}x_{k(i,m)}, with μi,m≠0\mu_{i,m}\neq 0. Since [xi,[xi,xj]]=0[x_{i},[x_{i},x_{j}]]=0 for all j∈Jj\in J and B⁡(𝔤)⊆ Span​{xj:j∈J}B(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq\text{ Span}\{x_{j}:j\in J\}, we know that [xi,[xi,B⁡(𝔤)]]=0[x_{i},[x_{i},B(\mathfrak{g})]]=0, so [xi,B⁡(𝔤)]=0[x_{i},B(\mathfrak{g})]=0 by ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3).

Moreover, by maximality of SS, [xi,xj]=0[x_{i},x_{j}]=0 for all j∈Jj\in J with j∉Sj\notin S. So if x∈B⁡(𝔤)x\in B(\mathfrak{g}) and x=∑j∈J​λj​xjx=\underset{j\in J}{\sum}\lambda_{j}x_{j}, then

0=[xi,x]=∑j∈J​λj​[xi,xj]=∑m∈S​λm​[xi,xm]=∑m∈S​λm​μi,m​xk⁡(i,m)0=[x_{i},x]=\underset{j\in J}{\sum}\lambda_{j}[x_{i},x_{j}]=\underset{m\in S}{\sum}\lambda_{m}[x_{i},x_{m}]=\underset{m\in S}{\sum}\lambda_{m}\mu_{i,m}x_{k(i,m)}

so since k⁡(i,m)≠k⁡(i,m′)k(i,m)\neq k(i,m^{\prime}) if m≠m′m\neq m^{\prime}, we see using linear independence that λm​μi,m=0\lambda_{m}\mu_{i,m}=0 for all m∈Sm\in S and hence λm=0\lambda_{m}=0. It follows that if T:=J\ST:=J\backslash S then x=∑j∈T​λj​xjx=\underset{j\in T}{\sum}\lambda_{j}x_{j}. Since this is true for all x∈B⁡(𝔤)x\in B(\mathfrak{g}), we deduce that B⁡(𝔤)⊆ Span​{xj:j∈T}B(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq\text{ Span}\{x_{j}:j\in T\}, and since SS is non-empty by assumption, TT is a proper subset of JJ.∎

Of course, the difficulty in utilising this result lies in finding the element i∈Ii\in I and the subset S⊆JS\subseteq J, and this issue must be dealt with separately for each example.

4.2 Positive root subalgebras

Again, let 𝔰\mathfrak{s} be a split semisimple Lie algebra over ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, with Cartan subalgebra 𝔥\mathfrak{h}, root system Φ\Phi and decomposition 𝔰=𝔫+⊕𝔥⊕𝔫−\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{n}^{+}\oplus\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{n}^{-}.

Let 𝔤:=𝔫+\mathfrak{g}:=\mathfrak{n}^{+}, and let {xα:α∈Φ+}\{x_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\} be the associated positive root basis for 𝔤\mathfrak{g}.

Now, recall that the positive system Φ+\Phi^{+} contains a unique highest root θ\theta (with respect to the Bruhat ordering), and the centre of 𝔤=𝔫+\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{n}^{+} is the one dimensional eigenspace 𝔰θ\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}. The following technical results allow us to apply Proposition 4.3 to root bases of this form.

Lemma 4.4.

Suppose Φ\Phi is an irreducible root system, not of type CC, and Ψ⊆Φ+\Psi\subseteq\Phi^{+} is any subset with θ∈Ψ\theta\in\Psi but Ψ≠{θ}\Psi\neq\{\theta\}. Then there exists α∈Φ+\alpha\in\Phi^{+} such that 2​α+β∉Φ2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi for all β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi, but α+γ∈Φ+\alpha+\gamma\in\Phi^{+} for some γ∈Ψ\gamma\in\Psi.

Proof.

As we will show, for many irreducible root systems Φ\Phi, we can choose a positive system Φ+\Phi^{+} such that for all α,β∈Φ+\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^{+}, 2​α+β∉Φ2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi. More generally, it would suffice to prove that for all α∈Φ+\alpha\in\Phi^{+}, β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi, 2​α+β∉Ψ2\alpha+\beta\notin\Psi, because in this case, since θ\theta is the unique highest root, it follows from [13, Lemma 3.2] that for all γ∈Ψ\gamma\in\Psi with γ≠θ\gamma\neq\theta, there exists α∈Φ+\alpha\in\Phi^{+} such that α+γ∈Φ\alpha+\gamma\in\Phi. Since we are assuming Ψ≠{θ}\Psi\neq\{\theta\} this completes the proof.

However, there are examples where there do exist pairs (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) of positive roots such that 2​α+β∈Φ2\alpha+\beta\in\Phi, so we will need to treat these cases separately. We will examine and eliminate each irreducible root system in turn, and we begin each example by realising each positive system as a set of real vectors. In all the examples below, {ei:i=1,…,n}\{e_{i}:i=1,\dots,n\} represents the standard basis for ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

  1. 1.

    Type AnA_{n}: We take Φ\Phi to be the set of all integer vectors in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} of length 2\sqrt{2} whose entries sum to 0. We can take Φ+={ei−ej:1≤i<j≤n}\Phi^{+}=\{e_{i}-e_{j}:1\leq i<j\leq n\}.

    For every α,β∈Φ+\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^{+}, writing α=ei−ej\alpha=e_{i}-e_{j}, β=ek−eℓ\beta=e_{k}-e_{\ell}, 2​α+β=2​ei−2​ej+ek−eℓ2\alpha+\beta=2e_{i}-2e_{j}+e_{k}-e_{\ell}, which can only lie in Φ+\Phi^{+} if i=ℓi=\ell and j=kj=k, implying that ℓ>k\ell>k, which is impossible. So 2​α+β∉Φ+2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi^{+} and the result follows as outlined above.

  2. 2.

    Type BnB_{n}: Since we are assuming that Φ\Phi does not have type CC, we know that it does not have type B2=C2B_{2}=C_{2}, so we may assume that n>2n>2. We can take Φ\Phi to be the set of integer vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} of length 1 or 2\sqrt{2}, and

    Φ+={ei−ej,ek,eℓ+em:i,j,n,k,ℓ,m≤n,i<j,ℓ≠m}\Phi^{+}=\{e_{i}-e_{j},e_{k},e_{\ell}+e_{m}:i,j,n,k,\ell,m\leq n,i<j,\ell\neq m\}

    In this case, it is possible that 2​α+β∈Φ+2\alpha+\beta\in\Phi^{+} for α,β∈Φ+\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^{+}, e.g. α=e2\alpha=e_{2}, β=e1−e2\beta=e_{1}-e_{2}, so we must look more carefully. However, if α=ei−ej\alpha=e_{i}-e_{j} for some i<ji<j, then 2​α+β2\alpha+\beta has either eie_{i} coefficient greater than 1, or eje_{j} coefficient less than −1-1, so 2​α+β∉Φ+2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi^{+}. Similarly, if α=ek+eℓ\alpha=e_{k}+e_{\ell} for k≠ℓk\neq\ell, then 2​α+β2\alpha+\beta has either eke_{k} or eℓe_{\ell} coefficient greater than 1, so 2​α+β∉Φ+2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi^{+}. So if 2​α+β∈Φ2\alpha+\beta\in\Phi then α=ek\alpha=e_{k} for some kk.

    If Ψ\Psi contains a root of the form γ=ei−ej\gamma=e_{i}-e_{j} with i<ji<j, then if j<nj<n, take α=ej+en\alpha=e_{j}+e_{n} and α+γ=ei−en∈Φ+\alpha+\gamma=e_{i}-e_{n}\in\Phi^{+}, and if j=nj=n then take α=eℓ+en\alpha=e_{\ell}+e_{n} for some i≠ℓ<ni\neq\ell<n (which we know exists since n>2n>2), and α+γ=ei+eℓ∈Φ+\alpha+\gamma=e_{i}+e_{\ell}\in\Phi^{+}. In either case, since 2​α+β∉Φ2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi, for all β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi, the result follows.

    Therefore, we may assume that Ψ\Psi does not contain a root of the form ei−eje_{i}-e_{j}, so every root in Ψ\Psi has the form eke_{k} or eℓ+eme_{\ell}+e_{m}. Therefore, if α=ek\alpha=e_{k} then 2​α+β2\alpha+\beta has eke_{k} coefficient at least 2 for every β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi, so 2​α+β∉Φ2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi. So 2​α+β∉Φ2\alpha+\beta\notin\Phi for all α∈Φ+\alpha\in\Phi^{+}, β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi, which completes the proof by the argument outlined above.

  3. 3.

    Type DnD_{n}: We take Φ\Phi to be the set of integer vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥4n\geq 4, of length 2\sqrt{2}, and

    Φ+={ei−ej,eℓ+em:i,j,ℓ,m≤n,i<j,ℓ≠m}\Phi^{+}=\{e_{i}-e_{j},e_{\ell}+e_{m}:i,j,\ell,m\leq n,i<j,\ell\neq m\}

    Again, for all α,β∈Φ+\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^{+}, if α=ei±ej,β=ek±eℓ\alpha=e_{i}\pm e_{j},\beta=e_{k}\pm e_{\ell}, then 2​α+β=2​ei±2​ej+ek±eℓ2\alpha+\beta=2e_{i}\pm 2e_{j}+e_{k}\pm e_{\ell}. Remark 4.6.

The proof of the results above assume we are making a particular choice of positive system in Φ\Phi. However, if we assume further that 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is algebraic, then up to isomorphism the nilpotent subalgebras 𝔫+\mathfrak{n}^{+} and 𝔫−\mathfrak{n}^{-} do not depend on the choice of positive system Φ+\Phi^{+}, since all Borel subalgebras of 𝔰\mathfrak{s} are conjugate under the action of the adjoint algebraic group. Therefore, since allowing the positive system to vary does not change 𝔤\mathfrak{g} (up to isomorphism), the following result does not depend on a fixed choice of Φ+\Phi^{+}.

Theorem 4.7.

If 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is the positive nilpotent subalgebra of a split semisimple algebraic Lie algebra 𝔰\mathfrak{s} over ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, and no irreducible component of 𝔰\mathfrak{s} has type CC, then B⁡(𝔤)=Z⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g})=Z(\mathfrak{g}).

Proof.

Using ( ∗ ⁣ ∗ ‣ 3.3), it is easy to show that if 𝔤=𝔤1⊕𝔤2\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_{1}\oplus\mathfrak{g}_{2} is a direct sum of two nilpotent Lie algebras, then B⁡(𝔤)=B⁡(𝔤1)⊕B⁡(𝔤2)B(\mathfrak{g})=B(\mathfrak{g}_{1})\oplus B(\mathfrak{g}_{2}) and Z⁡(𝔤)=Z⁡(𝔤1)⊕Z⁡(𝔤2)Z(\mathfrak{g})=Z(\mathfrak{g}_{1})\oplus Z(\mathfrak{g}_{2}). So we may assume that 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is indecomposable, and hence the associated root system of 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is irreducible, and not of type CC.

We know that Z⁡(𝔤)=𝔰θZ(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}, where θ\theta is the highest root in Φ+\Phi^{+}, and we also know that Z⁡(𝔤)⊆B⁡(𝔤)Z(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq B(\mathfrak{g}). Choose a subset Ψ⊆Φ+\Psi\subseteq\Phi^{+} such that B⁡(𝔤)⊆⨁α∈Ψ​𝔰αB(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq\underset{\alpha\in\Psi}{\bigoplus}\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha}, and we can assume that Ψ\Psi is minimal with respect to this property.

Since 𝔰θ⊆B⁡(𝔤)\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}\subseteq B(\mathfrak{g}), we know that θ∈Ψ\theta\in\Psi, so let us assume for contradiction that Ψ≠{θ}\Psi\neq\{\theta\}. Then using Proposition 4.5, we know that

  • •

    there exists α∈Φ+\alpha\in\Phi^{+} such that [xα,[xα,xβ]]=0[x_{\alpha},[x_{\alpha},x_{\beta}]]=0 for all β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi,

  • •

    we can choose a subset ∅≠Θ⊆Ψ\varnothing\neq\Theta\subseteq\Psi, maximal with respect to the property that [xα,xβ]≠0[x_{\alpha},x_{\beta}]\neq 0 for all β∈Ψ\beta\in\Psi, and

  • •

    k⁡(α,β)≠k⁡(α,β′)k(\alpha,\beta)\neq k(\alpha,\beta^{\prime}) for all β,β′∈Θ\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in\Theta, β≠β′\beta\neq\beta^{\prime}.

Applying Proposition 4.3, it follows that there exists a proper subset Ψ′\Psi^{\prime} of Ψ\Psi such that B⁡(𝔤)⊆⨁β∈Ψ′​𝔰βB(\mathfrak{g})\subseteq\underset{\beta\in\Psi^{\prime}}{\bigoplus}\mathfrak{s}_{\beta}, contradicting minimality of Ψ\Psi. Therefore, Ψ={θ}\Psi=\{\theta\}, so B⁡(𝔤)=sθ=Z⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g})=s_{\theta}=Z(\mathfrak{g}) as requried.∎

Remark 4.8.

This theorem is false if 𝔰\mathfrak{s} has type CC. For example, if it has type C2=B2C_{2}=B_{2}, then 𝔤=𝔫+\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{n}^{+} is 4-dimensional with basis {x0,x1,x2,x3}\{x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\} such that [x0,x2]=x3[x_{0},x_{2}]=x_{3}, [x0,x3]=x1[x_{0},x_{3}]=x_{1}, all other brackets zero. In this case B⁡(𝔤)= Span​{x1,x2,x3}B(\mathfrak{g})=\text{ Span}\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\} and Z⁡(𝔤)= Span​{x1}Z(\mathfrak{g})=\text{ Span}\{x_{1}\}.

Corollary 4.9.

Suppose GG is a pp-valuable group and 𝔤G\mathfrak{g}_{G} is a positive nilpotent subalgebra of a split semisimple algebraic Lie algebra over ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}, such that no irreducible component has type CC. Then all faithful prime ideals in K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).

Proof.

Using Theorem 4.7, we know that Z⁡(𝔤G)=B⁡(𝔤G)Z(\mathfrak{g}_{G})=B(\mathfrak{g}_{G}). So using Corollary 3.12 we see that all faithful prime ideals in K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).∎

4.3 Comparison to A⁡(G)A(G)

To assess how much of an improvement the method of using B⁡(G)B(G) is to studying prime ideals in K​GKG, we need to compare it to results obtained using A⁡(G)A(G).

As stated previously, if A⁡(G)=B⁡(G)A(G)=B(G) then this method constitutes no improvement, and this is the case for many examples, as the following result demonstrates.

Suppose 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a simple Lie algebra of type CnC_{n} for n≥2n\geq 2, and 𝔤=𝔫+\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{n}^{+}. Then B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}) is a maximal abelian ideal in 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of dimension (n+12)\binom{n+1}{2}.

Corollary 4.11.

If GG is a pp-valuable group and 𝔤=𝔤G\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_{G} is a positive nilpotent subalgebra of a split simple algebraic Lie algebra of type CnC_{n}, then B⁡(G)=A⁡(G)B(G)=A(G) has rank (n+12)\binom{n+1}{2}, while Z⁡(G)Z(G) has rank 1.

Proof.

We know 𝔤A⁡(G)\mathfrak{g}_{A(G)} is an abelian ideal of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} and B⁡(𝔤)=𝔤B⁡(𝔤)⊆𝔤A⁡(G)B(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{B(\mathfrak{g})}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}_{A(G)}. But 𝔤B⁡(𝔤)\mathfrak{g}_{B(\mathfrak{g})} is a maximal abelian ideal of dimension (n+12)\binom{n+1}{2} by Lemma 4.10, so it follows that 𝔤B⁡(𝔤)=𝔤A⁡(𝔤)\mathfrak{g}_{B(\mathfrak{g})}=\mathfrak{g}_{A(\mathfrak{g})}, and hence A⁡(G)=B⁡(G)A(G)=B(G), and they both have rank (n+12)\binom{n+1}{2}.

But Z⁡(𝔤)=𝔤Z⁡(G)=sθZ(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{Z(G)}=s_{\theta} has dimension 1, so Z⁡(G)Z(G) has rank 1.∎

So the B⁡(G)B(G) method affords no improvement if we assume that GG has type CC, but in light of Corollary 4.9, we know that it produces solid results in all other types. The only question remaining is, could a result such as this could be proved using the original A⁡(G)A(G)-method?

The short answer to this is no, because there are examples of groups GG given by Corollary 4.9 such A⁡(G)A(G) is strictly larger than the centre, so the original control theorem (Theorem 3.4) gives us a strictly weaker result.

For example, if GG is the group of unipotent, strictly upper triangular n×nn\times n matrices over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}, then 𝔤G\mathfrak{g}_{G} is a positive nilpotent subalgebra of type An−1A_{n-1}, but A⁡(G)A(G) consists of all matrices of the form (IkM0In−k)\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{k}&M\\ 0&I_{n-k}\end{array}\right) where k=⌊n2⌋k=\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor. If n>3n>3 then this is never central, so Theorem 3.4 does not imply our Conjecture A for this group, and we need to apply Corollary 4.9.

The following result generalises this example.

Proposition 4.12.

If 𝔤G\mathfrak{g}_{G} is the positive subalgebra of a split simple algebraic Lie algebra, then A⁡(G)≠Z⁡(G)A(G)\neq Z(G).

Proof.

Let Φ\Phi be the root system of the simple Lie algebra 𝔰\mathfrak{s}, Φ+\Phi^{+} the corresponding positive system, so 𝔤G=⨁α∈Φ+​sα\mathfrak{g}_{G}=\underset{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}}{\bigoplus}{s_{\alpha}}.

Using Lemma 3.6, we only need to check that Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is abelian, or equivalently Z2​(𝔤G)Z_{2}(\mathfrak{g}_{G}) is abelian. But if θ∈Φ+\theta\in\Phi^{+} is the highest root then Z⁡(𝔤G)=sθZ(\mathfrak{g}_{G})=s_{\theta}, so Z2​(𝔤G)=⨁α∈𝒵​𝔰αZ_{2}(\mathfrak{g}_{G})=\underset{\alpha\in\mathcal{Z}}{\bigoplus}\mathfrak{s}_{\alpha}, where

𝒵:={β∈Φ+: if ​α∈Φ+​ and ​α+β∈Φ​ then ​α+β=θ}\mathcal{Z}:=\{\beta\in\Phi^{+}:\text{ if }\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\text{ and }\alpha+\beta\in\Phi\text{ then }\alpha+\beta=\theta\}

So Z2​(𝔤G)Z_{2}(\mathfrak{g}_{G}) is abelian if and only if for all β,γ∈𝒵\beta,\gamma\in\mathcal{Z}, β+γ∉Φ\beta+\gamma\notin\Phi. We will calculate 𝒵\mathcal{Z} for each root system in turn, using the same positive systems that we used in the proof of Lemma 4.4 (we leave out type CC, since we calculated A⁡(G)A(G) in this case in Corollary 4.11).

  1. 1.

    Type AnA_{n}: θ=e1−en\theta=e_{1}-e_{n}, and 𝒵={e1−en,e1−en−1,e2−en}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{1}-e_{n},e_{1}-e_{n-1},e_{2}-e_{n}\}.

  2. 2.

    Type BnB_{n}: θ=e1+e2\theta=e_{1}+e_{2}, and 𝒵={e1+e2,e1+e3}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{1}+e_{2},e_{1}+e_{3}\}.

  3. 3.

    Type DnD_{n}: θ=e1+e2\theta=e_{1}+e_{2}, and 𝒵={e1+e2,e1+e3}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{1}+e_{2},e_{1}+e_{3}\}.

  4. 4.

    Type E8E_{8}: θ=e1−e8\theta=e_{1}-e_{8} and 𝒵={e1−e8,e2−e8}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{1}-e_{8},e_{2}-e_{8}\}.

  5. 5.

    Type F4F_{4}: θ=e1−e4\theta=e_{1}-e_{4} and 𝒵={e1−e4,e2−e4}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{1}-e_{4},e_{2}-e_{4}\}.

  6. 6.

    Type G2G_{2}: θ=3​δ+2​ε\theta=3\delta+2\varepsilon and 𝒵={3​δ+2​ε,3​δ+ε}\mathcal{Z}=\{3\delta+2\varepsilon,3\delta+\varepsilon\}.

We can also realise the roots of type E7E_{7} (resp. type E6E_{6}) as being the set of all roots in E8E_{8} where the first two (resp. 3) coordinates are equal. Therefore, we calculate:

  1. 1.

    Type E7E_{7}: θ=e3−e8\theta=e_{3}-e_{8}, and 𝒵={e3−e8,e4−e8}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{3}-e_{8},e_{4}-e_{8}\}

  2. 2.

    Type E6E_{6}: θ=e4−e8\theta=e_{4}-e_{8} and 𝒵={e4−e8,e5−e8}\mathcal{Z}=\{e_{4}-e_{8},e_{5}-e_{8}\}

We can immediately see, in all these examples, that taking the sum of any two vectors in 𝒵\mathcal{Z} will always leave 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.∎

4.4 Obstacles to a complete proof

While the methods outlined in this paper allow us to establish our Conjecture A for a wide range of new examples, they are still not sufficient to prove it in full generality, because there are still many examples of nilpotent groups GG such that B⁡(G)≠Z⁡(G)B(G)\neq Z(G), as demonstrated by Corollary 4.11, and also the following result.

Lemma 4.13.

Suppose GG contains a closed, isolated, abelian normal subgroup HH such that G/H≅ℤpG/H\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}. If GG has nilpotency class at least 3 then B⁡(G)=A⁡(G)=HB(G)=A(G)=H and B⁡(G)≠Z⁡(G)B(G)\neq Z(G).

Proof.

We will show that HH satisfies ( ∗ ‣ 3.2), and thus H⊆B⁡(G)⊆A⁡(G)H\subseteq B(G)\subseteq A(G) by definition. So since HH and A⁡(G)A(G) are both closed and isolated by Lemma 3.8, it follows that A⁡(G)=HA(G)=H or A⁡(G)=GA(G)=G. But GG is nilpotent, so A⁡(G)≠GA(G)\neq G by Lemma 3.3, thus A⁡(G)=B⁡(G)=HA(G)=B(G)=H.

Suppose g∈Gg\in G and (g,(g,H))=1(g,(g,H))=1. If g∈Hg\in H then (g,H)=1(g,H)=1 since HH is abelian, so assume for contradiction that g∉Hg\notin H. Then since G/H≅ℤpG/H\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we know that gg and HH generate an open normal subgroup UU of GG. Moreover, since (g,H)⊆H(g,H)\subseteq H, and gg and HH both commute with (g,H)(g,H), it follows that (U,(g,H))=1(U,(g,H))=1, i.e. (g,H)(g,H) is central in UU.

But (g,g)=1(g,g)=1 so this means that (g,U)(g,U) is central in UU by Lemma 2.1, and hence g∈Z2​(U)g\in Z_{2}(U). But Z2​(U)⊆Z2​(G)Z_{2}(U)\subseteq Z_{2}(G) by the proof of [8, Lemma 4.9]. So g∈Z2​(G)g\in Z_{2}(G), and since (H,H)=1(H,H)=1 this means that (U,H)⊆Z⁡(G)(U,H)\subseteq Z(G), so H⊆Z2​(U)⊆Z2​(G)H\subseteq Z_{2}(U)\subseteq Z_{2}(G), and hence U⊆Z2​(G)U\subseteq Z_{2}(G). This means that Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is an open normal subgroup of GG, so since it is isolated this implies that Z2​(G)=GZ_{2}(G)=G, contradicting the assumption that GG has nilpotency class at least 3.

So B⁡(G)=A⁡(G)=HB(G)=A(G)=H, and H≠Z⁡(G)H\neq Z(G) since GG is non-abelian and G/HG/H has rank 1.∎

To complete a proof of Conjecture A for nilpotent groups in general, it would be enough to establish that it holds for groups of the form ℤpd⋊ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{d}\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

We will conclude with some further examples, not arising from Lie theory and not covered by the previous cases. The following result suggests how we can try to employ an inductive strategy in the cases where A⁡(G)A(G) or B⁡(G)B(G) are too large, in particular circumventing the issue that A⁡(G)≠Z⁡(G)A(G)\neq Z(G) whenever Z2​(G)Z_{2}(G) is abelian.

Proposition 4.14.

Let 𝔥\mathfrak{h} be an ideal of 𝔤:=𝔤G\mathfrak{g}:=\mathfrak{g}_{G} containing 𝔤B⁡(G)\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)} (or 𝔤A⁡(G)\mathfrak{g}_{A(G)}). Suppose that B⁡(𝔥)=Z⁡(𝔥)=Z2​(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{h})=Z(\mathfrak{h})=Z_{2}(\mathfrak{g}). Then all faithful prime ideals of K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).

Proof.

Let UU be any open, normal subgroup of GG, then 𝔤U=𝔤G=𝔤\mathfrak{g}_{U}=\mathfrak{g}_{G}=\mathfrak{g}, while 𝔥=𝔤H\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{g}_{H} for some closed, isolated normal subgroup HH of UU. Moreover, B⁡(𝔤)=𝔤B⁡(U)=𝔤B⁡(G)B(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{B(U)}=\mathfrak{g}_{B(G)} by Proposition 3.11, so B⁡(U)⊆HB(U)\subseteq H, and B⁡(H)=Z⁡(H)=Z2​(U)B(H)=Z(H)=Z_{2}(U).

We know by Corollary 3.10 that all faithful primes in K​UKU are controlled by B⁡(U)B(U), and hence by HH. Let PP be a faithful prime ideal of K​UKU, and write P∩K​H=Q1∩⋯∩QnP\cap KH=Q_{1}\cap\dots\cap Q_{n}, where {Q1,…,Qn}\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{n}\} is a GG-orbit of prime ideals of K​HKH, and let Q=QiQ=Q_{i} be arbitrary. Then QQ is also faithful, and since B⁡(H)=Z⁡(H)B(H)=Z(H) it follows from Corollary 3.10 again that QQ is controlled by Z⁡(H)Z(H). It follows by a faithful flatness argument (cf. [4, Lemma 5.1]) that

(P∩K​Z​(H))​K​U\displaystyle(P\cap KZ(H))KU =((P∩K​H)∩K​Z​(H))​K​H⋅K​U\displaystyle=((P\cap KH)\cap KZ(H))KH\cdot KU
=(Q1∩⋯∩Qn∩K​Z​(H))​K​H⋅K​U\displaystyle=(Q_{1}\cap\dots\cap Q_{n}\cap KZ(H))KH\cdot KU
=((Q1∩K​Z​(H))∩⋯∩(Qn∩K​Z​(H)))​K​H⋅K​U\displaystyle=((Q_{1}\cap KZ(H))\cap\dots\cap(Q_{n}\cap KZ(H)))KH\cdot KU
=((Q1∩K​Z​(H))​K​H∩⋯∩(Qn∩K​Z​(H))​K​H)​K​U\displaystyle=((Q_{1}\cap KZ(H))KH\cap\dots\cap(Q_{n}\cap KZ(H))KH)KU
=(Q1∩⋯∩Qn)​K​U\displaystyle=(Q_{1}\cap\dots\cap Q_{n})KU
=(P∩K​H)​K​U=P.\displaystyle=(P\cap KH)KU=P.

Hence PP is controlled by Z​(H)=Z2​(U)Z(H)=Z_{2}(U). Since this is true for all open normal subgroups UU of GG, it follows from Proposition 2.16 that every faithful prime ideal of K​GKG controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).∎

The following example demonstrates how to make use of this result to improve the A⁡(G)A(G)-method (though in this case the B⁡(G)B(G)-method also works).

Example 4.15.

Suppose 𝔤:=𝔤G\mathfrak{g}:=\mathfrak{g}_{G} is the ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-Lie algebra generated by x1,…,x6x_{1},\dots,x_{6}, subject to the relations [x1,x2]=x3[x_{1},x_{2}]=x_{3}, [x1,x5]=x6[x_{1},x_{5}]=x_{6}, [x2,x3]=x4[x_{2},x_{3}]=x_{4}, [x2,x4]=x5[x_{2},x_{4}]=x_{5}, [x3,x4]=x6[x_{3},x_{4}]=x_{6}, and otherwise [xi,xj]=0[x_{i},x_{j}]=0.

Then 𝔤\mathfrak{g} has nilpotency class 5, and its upper central series is

Z⁡(𝔤)\displaystyle Z(\mathfrak{g}) =⟨x6⟩,\displaystyle=\langle x_{6}\rangle,
Z2​(𝔤)\displaystyle Z_{2}(\mathfrak{g}) =⟨x5,x6⟩,\displaystyle=\langle x_{5},x_{6}\rangle,
Z3​(𝔤)\displaystyle Z_{3}(\mathfrak{g}) =⟨x4,x5,x6⟩,\displaystyle=\langle x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle,
Z4​(𝔤)\displaystyle Z_{4}(\mathfrak{g}) =⟨x3,x4,x5,x6⟩,\displaystyle=\langle x_{3},x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle,
Z5​(𝔤)\displaystyle Z_{5}(\mathfrak{g}) =⟨x1,x2,x3,x4,x5,x6⟩.\displaystyle=\langle x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle.
  1. (i)

    Since Z2​(𝔤)Z_{2}(\mathfrak{g}) is abelian, it follows from Lemma 3.6 that A⁡(G)≠Z⁡(G)A(G)\neq Z(G). We can calculate A⁡(G)A(G) explicitly by defining the sequence A0⊇A1⊇A2⊇A_{0}\supseteq A_{1}\supseteq A_{2}\supseteq as a sequence of Lie algebra, as opposed to groups, and the intersection will yield A⁡(𝔤)=𝔤A⁡(G)A(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}_{A(G)}:

    A0\displaystyle A_{0} =⟨x1,x2,x3,x4,x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle Z2​(A0)\displaystyle Z_{2}(A_{0}) =⟨x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{5},x_{6}\rangle
    A1\displaystyle A_{1} =⟨x2,x3,x4,x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle Z2​(A1)\displaystyle Z_{2}(A_{1}) =⟨x4,x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle
    A2\displaystyle A_{2} =⟨x4,x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle Z2​(A2)\displaystyle Z_{2}(A_{2}) =⟨x4,x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle
    A3\displaystyle A_{3} =⟨x4,x5,x6⟩\displaystyle=\langle x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle …\displaystyle\dots

    and so the sequence has stabilised at A​(𝔤)=Z3​(𝔤)A(\mathfrak{g})=Z_{3}(\mathfrak{g}). Hence all faithful prime ideals P⊲K​GP\lhd KG are controlled by Z3​(G)Z_{3}(G) by [9, Theorem B]. Let 𝔥=⟨x3,x4,x5,x6⟩\mathfrak{h}=\langle x_{3},x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle, which has nilpotency class 2, with upper central series

    Z⁡(𝔥)\displaystyle Z(\mathfrak{h}) =⟨x5,x6⟩,\displaystyle=\langle x_{5},x_{6}\rangle,
    Z2​(𝔥)\displaystyle Z_{2}(\mathfrak{h}) =⟨x3,x4,x5,x6⟩=𝔥.\displaystyle=\langle x_{3},x_{4},x_{5},x_{6}\rangle=\mathfrak{h}.

    So since 𝔥\mathfrak{h} has nilpotency class 2, B⁡(𝔥)=Z⁡(𝔥)=⟨x5,x6⟩=Z2​(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{h})=Z(\mathfrak{h})=\langle x_{5},x_{6}\rangle=Z_{2}(\mathfrak{g}), so we can apply Proposition 4.14 to get that all faithful prime ideals in K​GKG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G).

  2. (ii)

    We can calculate B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}) as follows. Let y=α1​x1+⋯+α6​x6y=\alpha_{1}x_{1}+\dots+\alpha_{6}x_{6} be an arbitrary element of B⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g}). Then we calculate:

    • •

      [x1,[x1,y]]=0[x_{1},[x_{1},y]]=0 for any such yy, and hence [x1,y]=α2​x3+α5​x6=0[x_{1},y]=\alpha_{2}x_{3}+\alpha_{5}x_{6}=0, so α2=α5=0\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{5}=0.

    • •

      [x4,[x4,y]]=0[x_{4},[x_{4},y]]=0, and hence [x4,y]=−α3​x6=0[x_{4},y]=-\alpha_{3}x_{6}=0, so α3=0\alpha_{3}=0.

    • •

      [x5,[x5,y]]=0[x_{5},[x_{5},y]]=0, and hence [x5,y]=−α1​x6=0[x_{5},y]=-\alpha_{1}x_{6}=0, so α1=0\alpha_{1}=0.

    • •

      [x2,[x2,y]]=0[x_{2},[x_{2},y]]=0, and hence [x2,y]=α4​x5=0[x_{2},y]=\alpha_{4}x_{5}=0, so α4=0\alpha_{4}=0.

    Hence y=α6​x6∈Z⁡(𝔤)y=\alpha_{6}x_{6}\in Z(\mathfrak{g}), and so B⁡(𝔤)=Z⁡(𝔤)B(\mathfrak{g})=Z(\mathfrak{g}). Hence all faithful prime ideals P⊲K​GP\lhd KG are controlled by Z⁡(G)Z(G) by Theorem 3.10.

Unfortunately, we do not know any examples of groups GG for which the A⁡(G)A(G)-method succeeds using these refinements, but the B⁡(G)B(G)-method fails. In fact we conjecture that there are none, i.e. for any group GG where the condition of Proposition 4.14 is satisfied, we have B⁡(G)=Z⁡(G)B(G)=Z(G).
